title: Ingress/Egress Orchestration Sequencer and Trust Rotation
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a proposal and operational checklist for an orchestration layer we’re calling the ingress/egress sequencer. The sequencer’s goal is to deterministically order routing decisions, trust material rotation, and control-plane handoffs across regions so that latency SLOs, data isolation, and graceful failover are preserved during normal operation and during incidents (network partitions, region drain, cert rotation).

Scope and motivation:
- Problem observed: during region failover tests we saw cascading drops when control-plane actions (eg, config push + mTLS root rotation) were applied simultaneously across edge proxies and mesh data planes.
- Goals: minimize blackhole windows, avoid long-lived crypto mismatches, make shortest-path routing decisions consistent across tiered proxies, and provide clear fallbacks when a primary control plane is unreachable.
- Non-goals: replacing mesh implementation (we support both Istio-style and lightweight proxyless alternatives); not an access-control rewrite.

High-level architecture (sequencer concept):
1) Intent stage (control plane): a single authoritative sequencer instance (active-active across regions with leader lease per region) composes a stepwise plan for any operation that touches routing, certificates, or topology. The plan is versioned and includes minimal viable rollout units (MVUs) such as: single-edge-pop, AZ, full-region, or global.
2) Preflight checks: for each MVU the sequencer runs probes: health of local edge proxies, mesh-control-plane reachability (if present), KV cache priming success (see cache consistency checks), and policy validation (policy engine returns safe/unsafe).
3) Orchestrated apply: changes are applied MVU-by-MVU in a deterministic order. For region-level operations, the sequencer prefers: local-edge -> regional-egress-gateway -> mesh-control-plane -> origin-services.
4) Verification & rollback: after each MVU, staged verification occurs (synthetic traffic, cert handshake test, KV read/latency assertion). On failure, automatic rollback to previous plan is triggered.

Routing policy sequencing rules (practical principles):
- Edge-first for outward-facing changes: When changing egress CIDRs or external gateways, update edge routers before internal mesh so outbound TLS handshakes target the new egress path. This prevents client traffic from being blackholed by an unchanged internal gateway.
- Mesh-first for internal routing changes: For changes that affect service-to-service policies (eg, stricter mTLS requirements or new route weighting), prefer updating the mesh data plane before edge ingress to avoid accepting traffic that the mesh will reject.
- Affinity continuity: When moving traffic across regions, prefer session-affinity preserves for sticky routes (token ties to KV cache); if affinity cannot be maintained, sequencer advertises a short redirect window and supplies a migration token for replay.

mTLS and trust rotation approach:
- Staged root rotation: never rotate all roots at once. Use dual-trust windows: old-root + new-root accepted for a 24h period, with active probing to ensure no orphaned workloads. Sequencer schedules root rotation MVUs aligned with low-traffic windows for each region.
- Short-lived leaf certs + centralized issuance: rely on short-lived certs (1h-6h) issued by regional CA proxies; revocation handled via short TTLs and OCSP-like health tags maintained by control plane.
- Fallback behavior: if data plane reports >x% handshake failures post-rotation step, sequencer halts progression for dependent MVUs and flips affected edge proxies into a permissive-legacy-mode that accepts old roots for ingress only while blocking unapproved egress.

Service mesh considerations and sidecar alternatives:
- Two supported execution modes: sidecar-proxy (full mesh) and conduit-proxyless (lightweight). Sequencer templates separate orchestration steps for each.
- For sidecar meshes, ensure sidecar lifecycle hooks are coordinated so that proxy restarts do not simultaneously drop all PODs in an AZ. Use staggered rolling restarts with pod-batching policy tied to MVU size.
- For proxyless deployments, orchestration includes a small shim that performs TLS termination and KV cache priming to mimic sidecar guarantees during transition windows.

Cache priming and stateful dependencies:
- Problem: moving traffic between regions can cause sudden cache misses for KV-backed affinities and model KV caches used by inference serving.
- Approach: sequencer provides a pre-pass which issues warm-up probes (synth requests) to prime regional caches and validates hit-rate thresholds before cutover. For model KV caches we run probabilistic priming: select 1% of top keys to pre-populate then monitor miss-rate.

Multi-region fallback patterns and decision matrix:
- Local-failover: if an AZ fails, shift to region-local standby within same region (edge reroute). Sequence: edge -> local-egress -> mesh fallback -> service.
- Regional-failover: if a full region is degraded, route to nearest healthy region with capacity. Sequence: sequencer will first validate cross-region bandwidth and cache-lag budget; if budget insufficient, route to degraded-mode APIs (reduced feature set).
- Control-plane isolation: if leader sequencer in region loses quorum, fallback to cached plan with time-limited leases and an emergency-readonly routing mode that accepts only pre-approved routes.

Observability and SLO guards:
- Telemetry hooks: every MVU apply emits structured events to tracing and audit logs: sequencer.plan.id, mvus.step, ack timestamps, verification results, probe metrics.
- SLO guardrails: per-step latency and error thresholds; if overall 95th latency for synthetic traffic crosses threshold, sequencer rolls forward only after operator approval.

Runbook snippets (for SRE on-call):
- Scenario: cert rotation caused 12% handshake fails in eu-west-1 after MVU#3.
  1) Pause sequencer progress for eu-west-1.
  2) Flip edge proxies to permissive-legacy-mode via /ops/edge-toggle with MVU id.
  3) Re-run cert probe against representative mesh endpoints; collect tls debug logs.
  4) If root mismatch found, revert cert push for affected MVU and re-enroll leaf certs.
  5) Escalate to Applied ML if model-serving cache priming shows high miss spike.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How long should dual-trust windows be? Ops wants 24h, security favors minimum viable (2h). Need experiment to measure orphaned workload surface area.
- Sequencer leader election model: active-active across regions is nice for latency but increases complexity for cross-region consistent MVU ordering. Consider a single global leader with regional proxies to simplify ordering.
- Synthetic traffic coverage: what percentage of production callgraphs do we need to probe to be confident? 10%? 30%? cost vs confidence tradeoff.

Action items / near-term experiments:
- PLAT-1987: prototype MVU preflight probes for edge and cache priming (Diego assigned).
- infra PR: add permissive-legacy-mode toggle endpoint and audit trail (Samir assigned, see linked PR).
- Runbook update: add explicit cert-rollback checklist and sample curl/tls commands for on-call (Lena assigned).
- Experiment: two-week A/B of dual-trust durations (2h vs 24h) on low-traffic region, measure handshake orphan rate and operational toil.

Appendix: useful commands and probes
- tls probe (example): openssl s_client -connect <edge-host>:443 -CAfile new-root.pem -cert leaf.pem -key leaf.key -tls1_3
- cache priming: curl -H 'X-Priming: sequencer' https://edge-host/_prime?key=<id>
- sequencer API: POST /sequencer/v1/plan/apply {"plan_id":"...","mvu":"eu-west-1-az1"} (returns async op id)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft; looking for feedback particularly on leader election model and dual-trust duration.
- If you have real incident stories that map to the cache-priming idea, please paste them into the comments or link the incident ticket.
summary: Draft design for a sequencer that orders routing, trust rotation, and control-plane handoffs across regions to reduce blackholes and ensure safe rollouts. Includes rules for ingress vs mesh sequencing, staged mTLS rotation, cache priming, observability events, and runbook steps.
